source.title: Efficient Full-Matrix Adaptive Regularization
source.authors: Naman Agarwal; Brian Bullins; Xin-Yi Chen; Elad Hazan; Karan Singh; Cyril Zhang; Yi Zhang

record.tranche_reason: Optimizer comparisons on image and language tasks qualify the generalization comparison: results vary by task and adaptive optimizer, and GGT is a full-matrix method rather than the diagonal adaptive methods emphasized in V4.
record.gate_note: The paper's cited optimizer-generalization findings are prior work and are not rows. The paper reports its own GGT, Adam, and SGD comparisons; curves without stated numerical values are recorded as figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own adaptive-versus-SGD held-out performance comparisons on image classification and character-level language modeling, extending V4 to a full-matrix adaptive optimizer and additional architectures.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's empirical paraphrase is accurate but omits the paper's main conclusion: GGT makes full-matrix adaptive preconditioning practical and accelerates optimization in preliminary benchmarks. Its held-out advantage is task dependent: SGD remains better on the tested CNNs, GGT achieves the best reported LSTM validation perplexity, and Adam outperforms GGT on the Transformer.
record.recipe_differences: Compares a full-matrix adaptive optimizer, GGT, with diagonal adaptive methods and SGD on standard tasks; settings and tuning are not a direct replication of the optimizer comparisons in V4.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported optimizer ranking differs across CIFAR-10 residual CNN, CIFAR-10 VGGNet, PTB character-level LSTM, and PTB character-level Transformer. Learning-rate schedule and explicit Shake-Shake regularization are stated for the residual CNN; fixed halving schedule is stated for VGGNet.

fits_no_version.finding: On the character-level Transformer, Adam eventually outperforms GGT in training and validation loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relative performance of full-matrix and diagonal adaptive optimizers depends on architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: On word-level language modeling, GGT is competitive with Adam and improves performance only during approximately the first 20 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Full-matrix adaptivity provides limited lasting improvement over Adam on the tested word-level language models.

record.problems: The generalization results for CIFAR-10 and the Transformer are chiefly shown in plots, without numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. Comparisons are across different tasks and architectures, and the paper notes the residual CNN uses explicit regularization and a tuned, annealed learning rate.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible results omitted. Synthetic optimization convergence results do not measure the training-to-test generalization gap.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization under the same training recipe.
Width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.

Systematic broader hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching from Adam to SGD, and Adam-versus-SGD comparisons on word-level language models. The precise tuning search and matched training performance are not established for every comparison.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove large-batch penalties.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for V4. Its small residual-network gap supports the stated optimizer ranking; the authors attribute its reduced magnitude to learning-rate tuning and strong explicit regularization. No uncertainty estimates establish whether that small difference is statistically significant. The LSTM reversal challenges an extension to this setting, without refuting V4's qualified claim that adaptive methods often generalize worse.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
The paper does not test broad hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching from Adam to SGD, or the word-level language-model condition named in the version.
Large-batch comparisons and adaptations to batch size.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures.

rows.measure: Test accuracy / generalization relative to training loss
rows.note: The text says SGD generalized slightly better than all other optimizers toward the end of training, including GGT, and that the gap was <0.2%; it says GGT shrinks the gap slightly.
rows.check: Replace figure-only values with the text-reported SGD advantage of less than 0.2 percentage points over the other optimizers. The small magnitude does not make the effect incomplete: V4 specifies no minimum gap. The SGD comparator uses momentum 0.9.

source_check.correct: Absolute test accuracies are figure-only; the text reports an SGD advantage below 0.2 percentage points over the other optimizers despite GGT's lower training loss.

rows.subject: 3-layer LSTM
rows.operation_detail: Compared SGD, AdaGrad, Adam, and GGT on character-level Penn Treebank language modeling; validation perplexity reported.
rows.note: The stated validation perplexities show Adam and GGT outperforming SGD; GGT has the lowest stated perplexity.
rows.check: The reported validation perplexities support the extracted ranking. This is character-level language modeling, distinct from V4's explicit word-level exception.
